question:
How do I store Decimal() values coming from SQL in CSV file with Python?

I have a simple chatbot that generates SQL queries and uses them on a database. I want to store the output in a .csv file and then download that file. This is usually possible when I take my output from SQL (a list of dicts), create a pd.Dataframe after evaluating that output, and finally download it as a csv file using st.download_button. However, when the result is a Decimal() format from SQL, pd.Dataframe fails and both eval and literal_eval would not work on it (I got invalid object error using literal_eval). I also tried to convert the data using Python's Decimal datatype. from decimal import Decimal But this recognized the output object as string and not a Decimal. So I did some research and found that writerows would work with Decimal type data, but I am still not able to download the file. out = db.run_no_throw(query, include_columns=True) #This is the output returned by the database. According to the [docs][1], this returns a string with the result. print(out, type(out)) # Prints [{A: Decimal(1,2)}] and str (literal_eval(out), literal_eval(str(out)) and literal_eval('"' + out + '"') all gave an invalid object error here) This is how I am currently trying to download the output data: with open(filename, mode='w+', newline='') as file_to_output: writer = csv.writer(file_to_output, delimiter=",") writer.writerows(out) downloaded = st.download_button( label="Download data as CSV", data=file_to_output, file_name="filename.csv" ) The above code creates a file locally with the expected data, but it prints 1 line per row in the .csv file, like so - [ { A : D e ... However,
reference_answer: pandas .read_sql_query() method can be used to directly create a DataFrame from an SQL query. Then the DataFrame can be written to a CSV file using the .to_csv() method. import pandas as pd import sqlalchemy as sa engine = sa.create_engine("postgresql://scott:tiger@192.168.0.199/test") sql = """\ SELECT 'widget' AS item, CAST(2.99 AS Decimal(18, 4)) AS price UNION ALL SELECT 'gadget' AS item, CAST(9.99 AS Decimal(18, 4)) AS price """ df = pd.read_sql_query(sql, engine, coerce_float=False) print(df) """ item price 0 widget 2.9900 1 gadget 9.9900 """ print(repr(df.loc[0, "price"])) # Decimal('2.9900') df.to_csv("products.csv", header=True, index=False) with open("products.csv", "r") as csv: print(csv.read()) """ item,price widget,2.9900 gadget,9.9900 """
llm_attempt: Your database returns a string representation of a list. Parse it first with `ast.literal_eval()` or `json.loads()` to get actual dict objects, then use `csv.DictWriter` instead of `csv.writer`. The issue is that `writerows(out)` iterates over the string character-by-character because `out` is a string. Use: `parsed = ast.literal_eval(out)`, then create `DictWriter` with fieldnames from your dict keys, and call `writer.writerows(parsed)`. For the download button, read the file content and pass it to `data=` parameter as bytes or string.

question:
Flask publish on different local ip than the machine it deployed on inside a docker

I am using docker with a flask app inside to display the visual results in a browser. I have created the image with the flask inside, tested on my machine (an Ubuntu 24.04 machine) and it seems to work fine. Flask reports 2 ips (the localhost and the actual ip of my pc) which can be accessible from my machine (through a browser) or even from other machines (the port has been open in my machine). The problem I am facing is that when I try to deploy it on a server the same docker does not seem to work as expected. Let me summarise the issues I encounter: a) The reported ips are: * Running on all addresses (0.0.0.0) * Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000 * Running on http://172.17.0.2:5000 the first one is the localhost so it should be available from the same machine (if I am not mistaken) while the second one should be also accessible from a local network, right? I have exposed the port 5000 from within the docker (in both machines). Should I include the parameter: -p 5000:5000 when I run my docker for example? b) The reported second ip is a private ip also if I am not mistaken. I was expected a public ip to be exposed. In my first pc we have static ips, maybe this is the reason for not being able to see a public ip? c) If we suppose a public ip is not available, then a local one is provided. But it seems peculiar that it is not the server's ip. I am using another ip (another local one) to connect to the server via ssh: ssh username@172.22.10.10 How is it possible for flask to expose a different local ip than the actual ip of the machine it is deployed on (even on a docker)?
reference_answer: Although, @David Maze answer seem to cover most of the issues I encountered, I decided to publish my experience as I understand it, being a novice docker and flask user. Well, after a lot of trial and error I concluded that the flask reported ips are not so reliable when utilized inside a docker container. Since the docker does not have any way to know the host's ip. So, in order for the flask app to be accesible from the local network I needed these actions: a) Utilize the host's ip (the local one, at least in my case) even though the flask reported different local ip. So, I should have used the ip which was used to connect to the machine via ssh for example. b) Open an unused port in the host machine to be able to read the request. This should be linked to the host's port via the -p parameter when the image is being launched. If for any reason there is a statement of a used port then a different one should be used (and be opened in the host of course). c) Inside the docker dockerfile (I am not familiar with compose approach) there should be a: EXPOSE 5000 or whatever port the flask is using ( 5000 is the default one). This is the second part of the -p host_port:container_port parameter. d) The flask app should listen to 0.0.0.0 which correspond to all interfaces as David stated. The reported ips might be any internal container IP address and should not be taken literally. Even further, if specifically declared to listen on this internal IP (if being displayed at a first launch -using 0.0.0.0 - and then on a second launch specifically set to this IP) flask will complain wi
llm_attempt: The IPs shown represent: 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces), 127.0.0.1 (localhost), 172.17.0.2 (container's internal IP). To access Flask from outside the container, use `-p 5000:5000` flag when running the image. The 172.17.x.x IP is the container's private network address, not the host's. From another machine, connect to the host's IP on port 5000. To bind to a specific interface inside the container, pass `--host=0.0.0.0` to Flask (already done if seeing all addresses). The server IP (172.22.10.10) is the host machine's IP; containers have separate network interfaces.

question:
vscode breakpoints in an imported module do not work suddenly

I encountered a weird problem about vscode breakpoints for python in an imported module. The module is in the subfolder 'src' of the working folder of the main program 'main.py'. Then the main program does the following to import the module named cn.py. from src import cn I have a command near the top of cn.py to execute a print("YYY") Everthing works fine till this morning. Suddenly the vscode breakpoints in cn do not work anymore. I deleted my vscode and installed it again. The problem still persists. I copied main.py and cn.py to my colleagures. They found no problem with the breakpoints in cn.py in vscode. Can someone tell me what could go wrong? Your suggestions and comments will be highly appreciated.
reference_answer: OK, it was a stupid question. In the experiment of automatic updating binaries, I mistakenly downloaded a cn.pyd to src. Then I wasted almost a whole day trying to figure out why breakpoints in cn.py do not work trying this and that. Finally my colleagues suggseted me to check cn._ file _ and find out what I reallly imported. Maybe this experience could save someone's time in the future when they read this.
llm_attempt: Check your VSCode debug configuration: ensure the Python interpreter path is correct in settings.json or launch.json. Verify the module's path is in PYTHONPATH. Try: 1) Restart VSCode completely, 2) Check if debugpy is installed (`pip install debugpy`), 3) Clear .vscode/launch.json and recreate it, 4) Ensure you're debugging the correct Python executable. question:
How can I keep distincts data points with similar X value?

I have a dataframe with 4 rows, two of which having the same value for the "a" field. I'd like to have a bar chart with 4 bars, one for each row. Trying with Altair source = pd.DataFrame({ 'a': ['A', 'B', 'C', 'B'], 'b': [10, 20, 30, 15] }) alt.Chart(source).mark_bar().encode( x='a', y='b' ) This will result in a 3-bar chart, the values for 'B' having been added (20+15=35) What I was expecting is a 4-bar chart, like I get with: source.plot(kind="bar", x="a", y="b") If each value must be unique, I guess I could use the index of the dataframe, but I have not found any way to get the labels from the 'a' column. alt.Chart(source.reset_index()).mark_bar().encode( x='index:O', y='b' ) As expected, it brings the right values, but non the wanted labels: So it's possible to fake a column with unique values and trim the added part to get the proper labels back, but it seems not very pythonic to me. source["combined"] = source.index.astype(str) + "_" + source["a"] alt.Chart(source).mark_bar().encode( x=alt.X( "combined", axis=alt.Axis(labelExpr="slice(datum.label,indexof(datum.label, '_')+1)"), ), y="b", ) What would be the proper way to solve this?
reference_answer: You can create a new value that combines the index and a column and then splits them when generating the axis: alt.Chart(source).transform_calculate( label=alt.datum["a"] + "_" + alt.datum["index"] ).mark_bar().encode( alt.X("label:N", title="A").axis(labelExpr='split(datum.value, "_")[0]'), alt.Y("b"), )
llm_attempt: Altair aggregates duplicate x-values by default. Disable aggregation by adding `.encode(x=alt.X('a:N', aggregate=None))` or better, use the index as a unique identifier: `source.reset_index(drop=False)` then encode `x=alt.X('index:O')`  with custom labels. Or create a combined column: `source['id'] = source['a'] + '_' + source.index.astype(str)`, encode that, then use `axis=alt.Axis(labelExpr="slice(datum.value, ...")`. The simplest is adding `aggregate=None` to X encoding to preserve all rows.

question:
The result obtained from the OpenCV-Python cv.add() function differs from the official documentation

During my learning process of OpenCV-Python, I encountered an issue. My environment uses Python version 3.13, NumPy version 2.2.6, and OpenCV-Python version 4.12. In the "Arithmetic Operations on Images" section of the official documentation, it mentions the difference between OpenCV addition and NumPy addition: OpenCV addition is a saturated operation while NumPy addition is a modulo operation. Official documentation page However, the actual results I obtained during computation differ from the values provided in the documentation. My code: import cv2 as cv import numpy as np x = np.uint8([250]) y = np.uint8([10]) print(f"x+y = {x+y}") print(f"cv.add(x,y) = {cv.add(x,y)}") Official documentation result: [4] [[255]] My result: [4] [[260.] [0.] [0.] [0.]] I checked cv.add(x,y).dtype and found it returns float64 instead of uint8 . After attempting data type conversion and retrieving the first value with cv.add(x,y).astype(np.uint8)[0] , the result is [4], which matches the NumPy addition result. How can I obtain the correct value from the cv.add() algorithm?
reference_answer: There is a reported issue for this mismatch between documentation and actual behavior. As you pass 1D arrays to cv.add the interpretation within OpenCV may be ambiguous. The output [[260.], [ 0.], [ 0.], [ 0.]] suggests OpenCV is treating the input as a 4-channel vector (possibly RGBA), filling missing channels with zeros, and performing the addition channel-wise. To avoid ambiguity, use explicit 2D arrays (e.g., np.uint8([[250]]) ) or specify the shape. See also this answer . import cv2 as cv import numpy as np # Explicitly create a 1x1 image x = np.uint8([[250]]) y = np.uint8([[10]]) print(f"x+y = {x+y}") print(f"cv.add(x,y) = {cv.add(x,y)}") # Reshape to 1x1 image x = np.uint8([250]).reshape((1, 1)) y = np.uint8([10]).reshape((1, 1)) print(f"x+y = {x+y}") print(f"cv.add(x,y) = {cv.add(x,y)}") x+y = [[4]] cv.add(x,y) = [[255]] x+y = [[4]] cv.add(x,y) = [[255]]
llm_attempt: The cv.add() function returns float64 in your OpenCV/NumPy version combination due to type inference changes. Convert explicitly: `result = cv.add(x, y).astype(np.uint8)`. To get uint8 directly, ensure both inputs are uint8 and specify dtype: `result = cv.add(x, y, dtype=cv.CV_8U)` if the parameter exists in your version, or manually cast the result. Check your OpenCV version's documentation as behavior changed between versions 4.x. The official docs may reference older behavior; verify with your specific version (4.12).

question:
Where should I allocate the pool in Python multiprocessing?

I want to distribute a Python application over several kernels, and from the documentation, I understand that a pool is the way to do this. My problem can be reproduced by the following code: #!/usr/bin/python3 import multiprocessing as mp import multiprocessing.managers import time def poolswimmer(): for i in range(5): print(i) time.sleep(1) def poolprocess(_pool): res = _pool.apply_async(poolswimmer) res.wait() if __name__ == "__main__": mp.freeze_support() mpc = mp.get_context('spawn') manager = mpc.Manager() pool = manager.Pool() p = mp.Process(target=poolprocess, args=(pool,)) p.start() p.join() pool.close() The <poolprocess> is the I/O intensive part and <poolswimmer> is the CPU intensive part of a job which is executed in loops for different peripherals. I get the following error: Process Process-2: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/usr/lib/python3.12/multiprocessing/process.py", line 314, in _bootstrap self.run() File "/usr/lib/python3.12/multiprocessing/process.py", line 108, in run self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs) File "/home/dad/sandbox/ImageProcessing/poolrider.py", line 12, in poolprocess res = _pool.apply_async(poolswimmer) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "<string>", line 2, in apply_async File "/usr/lib/python3.12/multiprocessing/managers.py", line 827, in _callmethod proxytype = self._manager._registry[token.typeid][-1] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute '_registry' The object inspector tells me that my pool variable is an instance of a PoolProxy object, so it should be OK to call it from the proce
reference_answer: While the previous comments and answers were very helpful, it took me still quite some time to make them work for me. The main reason was that I had oversimplified the task in my original post. The task "poolswimmer" in my application is a class that contains data along with the processing functions. This worked very well when starting it as a threading.Thread , but when I made it a process, I ran into problems. multiprocessing.Pool transports the data to the referent by pickling the complete class, including the methods, and that fails for security reasons. I have solved this by handcrafting the transport of the data only with JSON content, like in this example: from cpool import CPool import multiprocessing as mp import multiprocessing.managers as m import json class Strange: def __init__(self, lst): self._lst = lst def __str__(self): return f"{[itm for itm in self._lst]}" class Packed: def __init__(self): self._num = 0 self._txt = "" self._flt = 0.0 self._lst = Strange([]) def populate(self, jdata): self._num = jdata['num'] self._txt = jdata['txt'] self._flt = jdata['flt'] self._lst = Strange(jdata['lst']) def prt(self): print("Content:") print(f"num: {self._num}, txt: {self._txt}, flt: {self._flt}, lst: {self._lst}") @classmethod def prepare_for_json(cls, num, txt, flt, lst): JData = {'num': num, 'txt': txt, 'flt': flt, 'lst': lst} return json.dumps(JData) @staticmethod def execute(jdat): target = Packed() target.populate(json.loads(jdat)) target.prt() if __name__ == "__main__": myp = CPool() targ1 = Packed.prepare_for_json(27, "Jo mei", 17.5, [2, 3, 4, 6]) targ2 = Pack
llm_attempt: Don't pass a managed Pool across process boundaries. The pool proxy loses manager context in child processes. Instead: 1) Create the pool directly in the main process (not via manager): `pool = mp.Pool()`, or 2) Create it inside poolprocess() using the same context. If you need sharing, use `mp.get_context('spawn').Pool()` directly. The manager-wrapped pool's state is unavailable to child processes. For your case, either make pool a global or pass the pool configuration parameters and reconstruct it in the child process.

question:
Django sign up page shows alert "Something went wrong, try again" instead of success message

I am working on Django project. I have a user_signup page where users can create an account. When I click Create an Account, and when i create it with users informations , instead of showing "signed up successfully" I get a browser alert "Something went wrong, try again" The page URL is http://127.0.0.1:8000/user_signup/ I want to show success message after successful signup views.py def user_signup(request): error="" if request.method=='POST': f=request.POST['fname'] l=request.POST['lname'] i=request.FILES['images'] p=request.POST['pwd'] e=request.POST['email'] con=request.POST['contact'] gen=request.POST['gender'] try: user=User.objects.create_user(first_name=f, last_name=l, username=e, password=p) StudentUser.objects.create(user=user, mobile=con, image=i, gender=gen, type=student) error="no" except: errror="yes" d={'error':error} return render(request, 'user_signup.html', d) html(user_signup) {% if user error == "no" %} <script> alert("Signup Successfully"); window.location("{% url 'user_login' %}") </script> {% endif %} {% if error =="yes"} <script> alert("Something went wrong, try again"); </script> {% endif %} what I am doing wrong, and how can i properly show a success message after signup ?
reference_answer: As I see, you had multiple small issues, not just one. In views.py: Typo: errror="yes" → should be error="yes" d was only defined in except but used in return return indentation was wrong type=student → should be a string: type="student" In the template: {% if user error == "no" %} → {% if error == "no" %} window.location(...) → window.location.href = ... {% if error =="yes"} → missing % So the views.py shall be: def user_signup(request): error = "" d = {'error': error} if request.method == 'POST': try: user = User.objects.create_user( first_name=request.POST['fname'], last_name=request.POST['lname'], username=request.POST['email'], password=request.POST['pwd'] ) StudentUser.objects.create( user=user, mobile=request.POST['contact'], image=request.FILES['images'], gender=request.POST['gender'], type="student" ) error = "no" except Exception: error = "yes" d = {'error': error} return render(request, 'user_signup.html', d) and for template: {% if error == "no" %} <script> alert("Inscription réussie !"); window.location.href = "{% url 'user_login' %}"; </script> {% endif %} {% if error == "yes" %} <script>alert("Erreur, réessayez");</script> {% endif %} That's all as I think
llm_attempt: You have multiple bugs: 1) Template variable typo: `'user error'` should be `'error'`, 2) `window.location()` is wrong—use `window.location.href` or `window.location` directly, 3) In views.py, typo: `errror` instead of `error`. Fix: context variable to `d={'error':error}`, and JavaScript to `window.location.href="{% url 'user_login' %}"`. Better approach: use Django's messages framework instead of alerts, or return a redirect response directly from the view with `messages.success()` to display on the next page.

Instead use: `def next(self) -> rx.vars.Var: return rx.redirect("/nextpage")`. Or in recent Reflex versions, store the redirect in state and check it in the component render. Check your Reflex version docs as the redirect pattern changed. If returning a redirect doesn't work, try using a computed var or state variable to trigger navigation after setting a flag.

question:
How to use the default value of a param when import a rule in Snakemake?

I am trying to generalize my snakemake workflow, but I see a weird behavior, which I am not sure if I am doing something wrong or if it is by default. I created a file analysis.smk rules and the evariable I tried to make a generic rule, to import it in many of my snakemake workflows, so I have, for instance in my analysis.smk rule: rule analysis: output: test.root input: input_test.root params: variable: "SvB" rebin: 10 shell: `python run_analysis.py {params.variable} {params.rebin}` In another Snakefile, I am importing this rule and using it as: module analysis: snakefile: "analysis.smk" config: config use rule analysis from analysis as run_analysis with: output: f"{config['output']}/hist.root" input: f"{config['output']}/input_hist.root" params: rebin: 20 And when I run my workflow, I am getting errors like: AttributeError: 'Params' object has no attribute 'variable', when formatting the following: Because I didn't define the variable . Is this expected? I would just like to change the value of some params, and use the default in others. I am using snakemake version 8.27.1
reference_answer: I'm using modules too and to my understanding when importing a rule and changing an element of it you are overwritting it. So you cannot just edit one part of it, its all or nothing.
llm_attempt: When overriding a rule with `use rule ... with:`, unmapped params aren't inherited from the original rule. You must provide all params that the rule needs. Set defaults in the rule definition: `params: variable='SvB', rebin=10` makes them accessible even if not overridden. Or in your override, specify all params: `params: variable='SvB', rebin=20`. This is expected behavior—only specified params are overridden; omitted ones don't inherit defaults from the imported rule. Always check the rule definition for required params.

question:
How to inject a global httpx.AsyncClient session in FastAPI using dependency injection?

I'm using FastAPI and want to share an httpx.AsyncClient session across requests using dependency injection. I followed a pattern using FastAPI's lifespan function and storing the session in app.state as follows: # Standard library imports from contextlib import asynccontextmanager from typing import AsyncGenerator, cast, Dict # Third party library imports import httpx from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, Depends @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncGenerator[None, None]: async with httpx.AsyncClient() as session: app.state.session = session yield async def get_session(request: Request) -> httpx.AsyncClient: return cast(httpx.AsyncClient, request.app.state.session) app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan) @app.get("/") async def root(session: httpx.AsyncClient = Depends(get_session)) -> Dict[str, int]: response = await session.get("https://www.stackoverflow.com") return {"status": response.status_code} if __name__ == "__main__": import uvicorn uvicorn.run(app) This works well, but I’m wondering: are there alternative approaches to injecting a shared httpx.AsyncClient session in FastAPI? What are the potential drawbacks of this pattern?
reference_answer: You can take a simpler approach by creating an httpx.AsyncClient as a singleton at the module level: client = httpx.AsyncClient() async def get_session() -> httpx.AsyncClient: return client This method is straightforward and avoids the need to deal with lifespan or store anything in app.state . But there's a key downside: the client never gets closed. That can lead to resource leaks over time, especially if you're using http2=True , persistent connections or DNS caching. In a production environment, this might eventually cause stability issues.
llm_attempt: Your approach is solid. Alternatives: 1) Use context vars: `contextvars.ContextVar()` for thread-local session storage, 2) Dependency injection with a factory function, 3) Use `request.app.state` directly without lifespan (but requires manual cleanup). Drawbacks of your lifespan approach: the session is tied to app lifecycle (good for cleanup), but you can't customize per-request. Advantages: automatic session reuse, guaranteed cleanup. For most use cases, your pattern is the recommended approach in FastAPI.

The text should be on top of the whole thing. But what it generates is a blank, unplayable video ( 2570 x 960 : why is the width 2570 ?); no errors, either. I've tried many combinations over the past few days, but none worked. reference_answer: The issue comes from these two lines bellow, resize asumes that only one of the arguments will be specified, meaning that the width argument is ignored (hitting this condition ) and because you didn't specify a size when calling CompositeVideoClip , the final clip will be rendered with the size of the first clip in the array (not documented but happens in this line ) which is most likely why you can't play the video . image_clip = resize(image_clip, width=1080, height=960) final_clip = CompositeVideoClip([image_clip, text_clip, video_clip]) Here you have it fixt. def generate_video(image_path, video_path, output_path, text, text_options=None): video_clip = VideoFileClip(video_path) video_clip = resize(video_clip, newsize=(1920, 1080)) video_clip = crop(video_clip, y1=1920 // 4, height=1920 // 2) image_clip = ImageClip(image_path, duration=video_clip.duration) image_clip = resize(image_clip, newsize=(1920, 1080)) image_clip = crop(image_clip, height=1920 // 2) default_text_options = { 'fontsize': 30, 'font': 'Arial', 'color': 'white', 'bg_color': 'black', } text_clip = TextClip(text, **(text_options or default_text_options)) text_clip = text_clip.set_duration(video_clip.duration) final_clip = CompositeVideoClip( [ image_clip.set_position((0.0, 0.0), relative=True), video_clip.set_position((0.0, 0.5), relative=True), text_clip.set_position(("center", "center")), # the last layer is the top layer ], size=(1920, 1080), ) final_clip.write_videofile(output_path, codec="libx264", audio=False) text_clip.close() image_clip.close() video_clip.close()
llm_attempt: The code is incomplete, but the issues are likely: 1) Missing `size` parameter in `CompositeVideoClip(clips=[...], size=(1080, 1920))`, 2) Not setting duration on all clips, 3) Missing `set_start()` to position clips vertically—you set x position but not y. Use `image_clip.set_position((0, 0))`, `video_clip.set_position((0, 960))` for vertical stacking. Specify final size explicitly in CompositeVideoClip. The width 2570 suggests clips aren't properly sized. Ensure all clips have defined durations matching the longest clip.
